{"concepts_used":["GC-0072","GC-0055","GC-0182","GC-0002","GC-0009","GC-0001","GC-0168"],"decline_reason":"","declined":false,"citations":[{"ref":"TMM/Part31/3#1~1","quote":"As such, and taking into account the presumption of registrability, a ground for rejection will generally only be appropriate under subsection 39(2) if a trade mark contains or consists of one or more of the signs prescribed and the presence of that sign would be likely to confuse the relevant public as to whether: the goods and services bearing the trade mark have a particular status given by legislation, or there is a connection between the applicant and the person, body, or organisation with whom the sign is associated."},{"ref":"TMA1995/s39(2)","quote":"(2) An application for the registration of a trade mark may be rejected if the trade mark contains or consists of:"},{"ref":"TMA1995/s39(2)(a)","quote":"(a) a sign that is prescribed for the purposes of this subsection; or"},{"ref":"TMA1995/s43","quote":"An application for the registration of a trade mark in respect of particular goods or services must be rejected if, because of some connotation that the trade mark or a sign contained in the trade mark has, the use of the trade mark in relation to those goods or services would be likely to deceive or cause confusion."}],"answer":"**Generally, yes under the Manual’s practice—but that is not an express statutory requirement of subsection 39(2).**

• **Manual practice:** A prescribed sign does not, by itself, generally justify a subsection 39(2) objection. The Manual says an objection will generally only be appropriate where the sign’s presence would be likely to confuse the relevant public about a legislative status of the goods or services, or a connection between the applicant and the person, body or organisation associated with the sign. This is an assessment of likely confusion, not a requirement to prove that someone has actually been confused. [1]

• **Act:** The supplied wording of subsection 39(2) says an application **may** be rejected if the mark contains or consists of a prescribed sign. That wording does not expressly make likely deception or confusion an additional condition. The Manual’s approach guides the exercise of that discretion; it is not legislation. [2–3]

• **Separate section 43 ground:** If rejection is considered under section 43, the Act expressly requires likely deception or confusion arising from a connotation of the mark or a sign within it, in relation to the particular goods or services. Where that statutory test is met, rejection is mandatory. [4]"}
